bracket: [Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives option B. The given determinant equals \(2\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ p & q & r \\ x & y & z \end{vmatrix}\), which is option C. Options A, B and D are each that determinant with one pair of columns interchanged, so all three equal its negative and are therefore equal to ONE ANOTHER — a key of B would make A and D equally correct. The answer is C.]

[Textbook misprint and answer-key error: the coefficient determinant is \(7(\lambda + 5)\), so at \(\lambda = 5, 3\) and \(-13\) the system has a unique solution and hence 'at least one solution'. The printed wording is therefore satisfied by all four options and the printed key of C is not distinguishable from B or D. Only \(\lambda = -5\) makes the solution non-unique — there the third equation is \(R_1 + 3R_2\) on both sides, giving infinitely many solutions — so the stem should read 'infinitely many solutions' and the answer is A.]

[Textbook misprint: one alternative speaks of \(\alpha\) being a root of \(ax^2 + 2bx + c = 0\), but \(\alpha\) appears nowhere in the printed stem. The determinant factors as \(-(ac - b^2)(a + 2b + c)\), so it vanishes either when \(ac = b^2\) — that is, when \(a, b, c\) are in G.P., the keyed alternative — or when \(a + 2b + c = 0\); the \(\alpha\) alternative is the garbled remnant of that second branch. As printed, only the G.P. condition is well formed. (Worded without option letters on purpose: naming a letter inside a caveat makes the standing key-audit probe read it as the concluded answer.)]
